Men marry because they're weary; women because they're curious. Both discover disappointment.”

“I doubt I'll ever marry, Harry. I'm too much in love. That's one of your aphorisms. I'm applying it, as I do everything you say.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a moment.

“An actress,” Dorian Gray answered, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “A rather conventional beginning.”

“You wouldn't think that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard of her.”

“Nobody has. But they will one day. She's a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are the decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they express it charmingly. Women embody the victory of matter over mind, just as men embody the victory of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you?”

“My dear Dorian, it's entirely true. I'm analyzing women at present, so I ought to know. The subject isn't as obscure as I expected. Ultimately, I find there are only two sorts: the plain and the painted. Plain women are extremely useful. If you want a reputation for respectability, you need only escort them to supper. The others are very charming, but they make one mistake. They use makeup to look young. Our grandmothers used it to try to speak brilliantly. Rouge and wit once went together. That's finished now. So long as a woman can look ten years younger than her daughter, she's completely satisfied. As for conversation, only five women in London are worth speaking to, and two of them aren't welcome in respectable society. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Oh, Harry, your opinions terrify me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“Roughly three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I'll tell you, Harry, but you must be sympathetic. After all, it would never have happened if I hadn't met you. You filled me with a wild hunger to know everything about life. For days afterwards, something seemed to beat through my veins. Lounging in the park or strolling along Piccadilly, I watched each person who passed and wondered, with a frantic curiosity, what sort of life they led. Some fascinated me; others filled me with dread. There was an exquisite poison in the air. I was passionate for sensations....

You will be pleased to learn that the undertaking which inspired such gloomy forebodings in you has begun without mishap. I reached this place yesterday, and my first employment is to reassure my dear sister that I am well and increasingly confident of success.

Already I am far to the north of London. Walking through the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a chill northern wind against my face, strengthening my nerves and filling me with pleasure. Can you comprehend the sensation? The breeze comes from the very regions towards which I travel, offering an advance taste of their icy climate. Encouraged by this promising wind, my dreams grow more ardent and distinct. In vain do I attempt to convince myself that the pole is a realm of cold and desolation; my imagination continually pictures a country of loveliness and joy. There, Margaret, the sun never disappears: its wide disk grazes the horizon and sheds unending radiance. There—for, with your permission, sister, I shall place some faith in earlier voyagers—snow and frost are excluded. A tranquil sea may bear us towards a land whose wonders and beauty exceed those of every inhabited region yet discovered. Its natural productions and landscape may have no parallel, just as the appearances of the heavenly bodies in those unexplored solitudes assuredly have none. What cannot be hoped for in a land of everlasting light? Perhaps I shall find the extraordinary force that draws the compass needle, and bring order to a thousand astronomical observations whose apparent irregularities need only this voyage to become permanently intelligible. I shall satisfy my burning curiosity by beholding a part of the globe no traveller has seen, and may walk on ground never marked by a human foot. Such attractions suffice to overcome every fear of peril or death and make me begin this difficult journey with the delight of a child setting off in a small boat with holiday companions to explore his native river. Yet even if every conjecture proves mistaken, you cannot deny the immeasurable service I may render humanity, down to its final generation, by finding a passage near the pole to countries now requiring months to reach; or by discovering the magnet's secret, a discovery possible, if at all, only through an expedition like mine.

These thoughts have quieted the agitation with which I opened my letter. My heart glows with an enthusiasm that lifts me heavenward, for nothing so calms the mind as a settled purpose, an object upon which the soul can steadily direct its intellectual gaze.

Dawn had arrived when I put the manuscript down. The rain had nearly stopped. The world looked gray and sorrowful, and the exhausted storm seemed to sigh and sob itself to sleep. I went to the stranger's room and listened outside his partly open door. Hearing his voice, I knocked. He did not answer, but he continued speaking. I looked in. He lay on his back, talking in broken but energetic phrases and emphasizing them by tossing his arms restlessly, as people do when delirious with illness. I entered quietly and leaned over him. He went on muttering and calling out. I spoke a single word to get his attention. At once his glassy eyes and pale, ashen face lit up with joy, gratitude, and welcome.

“Oh, Sandy, you've finally come! How I've longed for you! Sit beside me. Don't leave me. Never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where's your hand? Give it to me, dear. Let me hold it. There, now everything's right, everything's peaceful, and I'm happy again. We're happy again, aren't we, Sandy? You look so faint and unclear, like mist or a cloud. But you're here, and that's happiness enough. And I have your hand. Don't pull it away. It's only for a little while; I won't need it long.... Was that the child? Hello-Central!... She doesn't answer. Perhaps she's asleep? Bring her when she wakes. Let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say goodbye.... Sandy! Yes, you're there. My thoughts wandered for a moment, and I thought you'd gone.... Have I been ill long? I must have been. It feels like months. And the dreams! Such strange, terrible dreams, Sandy! They seemed as real as life itself. Delirium, of course, but so real! I thought the king was dead. I thought you were in Gaul and couldn't come home. I thought there had been a revolution. In the wild madness of those dreams, I thought Clarence and I and a few of my cadets had fought and wiped out all England's knights. Yet even that wasn't the strangest part. I seemed to belong to some distant age that hasn't been born yet, centuries in the future. That felt just as real as everything else. Yes, I seemed to have flown backward from that time into our own, then forward again. I was left there, a lonely stranger in that unfamiliar England, with a gulf of thirteen centuries between you and me! Between me and my home and friends! Between me and everything I love, everything that could make life worth living!
